group.title: Social life
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A person you spend time with or travel with.
examples: Her dog has been her loyal {companion} for ten years.
wrong: My companion on the trip was a stranger I never met.

words.meaning: The pleasant feeling of having friendly people around you.
examples: Many older people join clubs for {companionship}.
wrong: She wanted companionship, so she moved to an empty island alone.

words.meaning: A person of the same age or social group as you.
examples: Teenagers often care most about what their {peers} think.
wrong: The five-year-old’s peers were all retired grandparents.

words.meaning: The small group of people who are the most popular and fashionable.
examples: At school, he always wanted to be part of the {in-crowd}.
wrong: The in-crowd was the group nobody liked or noticed.

words.meaning: The happy feeling of being accepted as part of a group.
examples: Joining the choir gave her a sense of {belonging}.
wrong: His sense of belonging made him feel like an outsider everywhere.

words.meaning: Friendly and easy to talk to.
examples: Our new manager is very {approachable}, so people ask her for help.
wrong: He is so approachable that everyone is afraid to speak to him.

words.meaning: To spend time with other people for fun.
examples: I like to {socialize} with my colleagues after work.
wrong: He socializes by staying at home alone every night.

words.meaning: Meeting people to build useful contacts, especially for work.
examples: The conference is great for {networking} with people in the industry.
wrong: Networking means avoiding everyone at a business event.

words.meaning: A shy person who stays at the side at a party and does not join in.
examples: At dances, he was a {wallflower} who never asked anyone to dance.
wrong: The wallflower danced in the middle of the room all night.

words.meaning: A lively person who makes a social event fun for everyone.
examples: With her jokes and stories, she’s always the {life of the party}.
wrong: He was the life of the party, sitting silently in the kitchen all night.

words.meaning: A meeting of people, often for a social reason.
examples: We had a small family {gathering} for Grandma’s birthday.
wrong: The gathering was one person sitting alone.

words.meaning: An informal meeting of friends or family.
examples: We’re having a {get-together} on Saturday; come along!
wrong: The get-together was a formal exam in a silent hall.

words.meaning: A meeting of people who have not seen each other for a long time.
examples: Our school {reunion} is twenty years after graduation.
wrong: The reunion was the first time the strangers had ever met.

words.meaning: To move around and talk to different people at a social event.
examples: At the party, try to {mingle} and meet new people.
wrong: She mingled by staying in one corner and talking to nobody.

words.meaning: A person you bring with you to an event you were invited to.
examples: The invitation says I can bring a {plus-one} to the wedding.
wrong: My plus-one was a guest I left at home.

words.meaning: Shared by two or more people.
examples: We met through a {mutual} friend.
wrong: Their respect was mutual: she admired him, but he looked down on her.

words.meaning: The quality of staying faithful to a friend or group.
examples: His {loyalty} to his friends is unshakeable.
wrong: She showed loyalty by telling everyone her friend’s secrets.

words.meaning: To hurt someone who trusted you, for example by telling their secrets.
examples: He {betrayed} his best friend by lying about him.
wrong: She betrayed her friend by keeping his secret safe.

words.meaning: A small, close group that does not let others join easily.
examples: The popular girls formed a {clique} that ignored everyone else.
wrong: The clique welcomed anyone who wanted to join.

words.meaning: A person who is not accepted as part of a group.
examples: At first, he felt like an {outsider} in the small town.
wrong: The outsider was the most accepted member of the group.

words.meaning: To keep someone out of a group or activity.
examples: It’s unkind to {exclude} her from the game.
wrong: They excluded him by inviting him to everything.

words.meaning: Feeling alone and without contact with others.
examples: Working from home made him feel {isolated}.
wrong: She felt isolated because she was surrounded by friends all day.

words.meaning: The sad feeling of being alone without friends.
examples: Video calls helped her {loneliness} during the long winter.
wrong: His loneliness came from having too many friends around.

words.meaning: Support and unity between people with the same aims.
examples: The workers stood together in {solidarity}.
wrong: They showed solidarity by refusing to help each other.

words.meaning: The state of belonging to a club or group.
examples: My gym {membership} costs thirty dollars a month.
wrong: His membership means he is not part of the club.

words.meaning: To slowly become less close to someone over time.
examples: We {drifted apart} after she moved to another city.
wrong: They drifted apart and became closer than ever.

words.meaning: No longer in contact with a family member or friend because of a quarrel.
examples: He has been {estranged} from his brother for ten years.
wrong: She is estranged from her sister, so they talk every day.

words.meaning: To admire and respect someone.
examples: Younger players {look up to} her as a role model.
wrong: He looks up to his coach, so he has no respect for her.

words.meaning: To like each other immediately.
examples: Jack and Sam {hit it off} the moment they met.
wrong: We hit it off and couldn’t stand each other.

words.meaning: With members who care for and support each other strongly.
examples: They live in a {close-knit} community where everyone helps.
wrong: The close-knit family hardly knew or cared about each other.

words.meaning: Always together; too close to be apart.
examples: The two sisters have been {inseparable} since childhood.
wrong: They were inseparable, so they never saw each other.

words.meaning: A person you trust with your secrets.
examples: Her aunt was her closest {confidant}.
wrong: He told his confidant nothing because he didn’t trust him.

words.meaning: The group of people you are friends with.
examples: Her {circle of friends} grew when she joined the club.
wrong: His circle of friends was a list of people he had never met.

words.meaning: To stop being in contact with someone.
examples: We {lost touch} after high school.
wrong: We lost touch, so we message each other every day.

words.meaning: Friendly to people who arrive or join.
examples: The neighbors were very {welcoming} when we moved in.
wrong: The welcoming hosts told us to go away.

words.meaning: To become a friend of someone.
examples: She {befriended} the new girl on her first day.
wrong: He befriended his neighbor by never speaking to him.

words.meaning: To ignore someone on purpose in an unfriendly way.
examples: She {snubbed} me at the party and talked only to my sister.
wrong: He snubbed her by greeting her warmly and hugging her.

words.meaning: A party for friends after you move into a new home.
examples: We’re having a {housewarming} on Friday to show off the new apartment.
wrong: The housewarming was held the day they moved out for good.

words.meaning: The friendly feeling between people who spend time or work together.
examples: There was great {camaraderie} among the players.
wrong: The camaraderie on the team meant nobody trusted anybody.

words.meaning: Liking to talk a lot in a friendly way.
examples: Our {chatty} neighbor always stops to talk.
wrong: The chatty girl hardly said a word all evening.
